body.text: “Traitor, traitor,” screamed a crowd of All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (AIADMK) supporters near the Dharapuram Revenue Divisional Office (RDO), on September 16, as the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) candidate, P. Sathyabama, filed her nomination in front of the Returning Officer, A. Felix Raja, and exited the building.
“It was a tense stand-off as TVK supporters on one side and AIADMK cadre on the other began screaming at one another,” said Sivapragasam, a technical assistant in a local government project.

Dharapuram is a one-road town, with all major offices located on either side of the road that connects the textile town of Tiruppur with the temple town of Madurai. The campaign offices of the three major political parties that have fielded candidates for the October 6 byelections—the AIADMK, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), and the TVK—are situated about 50 metres from one another.

The fact that all offices were close by contributed to the tensions. There is only one way in and out of the RDO office, and the TVK candidate was exiting as the AIADMK candidate was on her way to file her nomination. “The anger in the voices of the AIADMK supporters was palpable,” Sivapragasam added. The AIADMK viewed Sathyabama as a traitor because she had won the May 2026 Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly elections as an AIADMK candidate. She was among the four from the AIADMK who resigned barely a fortnight after being elected to the State Assembly. In that poll, the DMK candidate was placed second, and the TVK candidate was a distant third.

Senior leaders from both the AIADMK and the TVK, who were part of the entourage of both candidates, helped avert clashes. It appears that this is the narrative that the AIADMK is trying to build on the ground. “Will you vote for a traitor, who backstabbed the party?” AIADMK’s former Minister Pollachi Jayaraman, asked voters in Kuppannan Koil, even as a small crowd cheered him on.

Sathyabama, who spoke to reporters after the incident, claimed that she did not have any choice but to quit. “The decision of the AIADMK general secretary to seek an alliance with the DMK was the reason for my resignation,” she said. This is the reason that all the MLAs who quit have advanced. This was also the line of argument of all the AIADMK dissidents who broke ranks with the party and voted in favour of the TVK in the confidence vote on May 13.

After a delay of two days, the Dharapuram Police on September 18 booked the AIADMK candidate K. Banumathi and eight others, including party leaders Pollachi Jayaraman and Dindigul Srinivasan, for allegedly damaging the car belonging to the TVK candidate, P. Sathyabama, and using foul language.

The incident repeated on September 20, as Sathyabama began her campaign in Kundadam union in Dharapuram. Even as she began canvassing for votes in the town, a group of people on one side began shouting “traitor”. Later, a few others from the other side of the road started raising slogans against Sathyabama. She tried talking back to them, claiming that it was the coming together of the DMK and the AIADMK that led to her decision. But nobody listened, and she was repeatedly interrupted by the crowd. To avoid escalation, she left the spot immediately.

While campaigning is yet to peak in the State, the AIADMK has also sent a strong message to its senior leaders who had stepped out of line. It is using the election to convey to its cadre how it views the recent organisational indiscipline and other issues within the party. The AIADMK high command has decided that barring its general secretary Edappadi K. Palaniswami and those loyal to him, no one else deserves to campaign. The list of star campaigners features 13 legislators.

Those AIADMK MLAs who voted for the TVK in the May 13 confidence motion in the Assembly, have been largely kept out. The leaders of the dissidents, Coimbatore strongman S.P. Velumani, and two other former Ministers, C. Ve. Shanmugham and Natham R. Viswanathan, are not in the list of star campaigners released by the party on September 18.

All top leaders in the State are expected to campaign, which is unusual for a byelection. This shows the importance that the main political parties have attached to the election. Palaniswami has announced that he will spend at least three days each in both constituencies. DMK president M.K. Stalin has also told the media that he will campaign in both the constituencies. Given the keen contest that is on the cards, Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay is scheduled to campaign in both constituencies for two days each. TVK’s coalition partners will also join the campaign.
Opposition parties make their moves

Senior leaders of the DMK have already fanned out across the constituency and hope that the party will be able to win the seat that it had won in 2021. This time, the DMK faces the poll without most of its allies from 2021 and 2026. The party’s candidate, 31-year-old S. Suganya, belongs to a family of local DMK leaders. Her mother was the village panchayat president. Suganya is a lawyer and grew up in Tavalaipalayam, on the outskirts of Dharapuram. The party is emphasising on the fact that she is a local and a “common person” who had been with the DMK through thick and thin.

The party, which had a sluggish start to the election, now fancies its chances. Former Minister M.P. Saminathan, a confidant of DMK president M.K. Stalin, who has been given charge of the constituency, has also latched on to the AIADMK campaign that Sathyabama’s act of moving to the TVK and resigning her seat made her a traitor.

Local leaders of both the AIADMK and the DMK told this correspondent that the byelection would be a good gauge of Vijay’s popularity. “One thing I have noticed is that there are no children telling their parents who to vote for,” says DMK district secretary Ela Padmanabhan. “This is a major change and it did not even take five months [for the change],” he added, referring to the 2026 May general election.

In the post-2026 election scenario, all political parties have upped their social media game too. But social media is just one part of the game. The TVK is acutely aware of its lack of ground infrastructure. In a hurried move, it made the candidate, Sathyabama, the local district secretary. This has not gone down well with the local TVK cadre. Besides, two senior TVK leaders, both of whom moved from the AIADMK—Minister K.A. Sengottaiyan and former Minister Udumalai Radhakrishnan—are encouraging AIADMK union secretaries to join the TVK.

One source told this correspondent that as of September 19, two of the four AIADMK union secretaries have begun working in tandem with the TVK. The AIADMK’s Dharapuram town secretary is also being encouraged to shift to the TVK. Initially, all the four union secretaries and the town secretary are said to have refused to move to the TVK. The reason was that Radhakrishnan, who moved to the TVK from the AIADMK, was not given any formal position.

Radhakrishnan was AIADMK’s district secretary (Tiruppur Suburban West) and was removed by Palaniswami after the May 2026 elections. Miffed, he along with former Minister M.C. Sampath, joined the TVK. Sampath too is waiting for a position after switching sides.

Another source said that the union secretaries were left with no option after they realised that some of their panchayat level leaders have joined the TVK. As of September 19, as many as 17 such leaders have left the AIADMK and joined the TVK, one local leader said. The DMK alleges that such large-scale movement of local-level leaders from one party to another can only happen with inducements; not ideology.

The TVK dismisses the claim of inducements as just small talk. “The TVK will win this seat. That is why the opposition is floating a false narrative from now itself,” said Radhakrishnan. “After all, they have to find something to say after the elections, right,” he asked.

The others in the fray are the Naam Tamilar Katchi’s (NTK) M. Karthika and the Communist Party of India’s (CPI) P. Lakshmanan. The CPI candidate is a construction worker, and belongs to Dharapuram. Both the Left parties have come in for considerable criticism because they have decided to contest the polls, while supporting the TVK government from outside. Speaking to Frontline, the journalist Jenram wondered: “In a scenario where the Left parties win both the seats, what will these MLAs do? Will they also support the TVK government from the outside.” The fact that the MLAs won by fighting the TVK will not be lost on the people, he contended.

The Pattali Makkal Katchi has declared that it will not support any party in the by-election. While NTK has never shied away from contesting an election, many political analysts in the State find it significant that both the Left parties have joined the fray. Many theories are being advanced. One claims that the average communist voter will find it difficult to vote for the TVK. There is a possibility that he or she would prefer the DMK from the field of candidates available. Another school of thought is that the Left parties wanted to assert their independence though they support the TVK government.

Left leaders said that they were contesting because the parties were not in alliance with the TVK. “There was a situation on May 10 wherein the BJP and the governor might have hijacked the people’s mandate. Our aim was to give a stable government in Tamil Nadu as per the wishes of the people. Since the TVK had the largest number of MLAs (107), we decided to support them in the interests of the State,” senior State Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPI(M)) leader K. Kanagaraj told Frontline. “We support the government. But that does not mean that we blindly accept all decisions of this government. Whenever there has been a problem in policy or an action, we have made our objections clear,” he added.

Leaders of the Left parties also told this correspondent that they could not support the TVK in the by-elections because of several incidents of wrongdoing on the part of the government. At the same time, it was not ethical on their part to support an opposition candidate. They dismissed the claim that by contesting, the CPI and CPI(M) were actively trying to ensure that the votes of their cadre did not favour the DMK candidate.

Unlike the Erode East byelection of 2025, where voter bribery was rampant, there is no such complaint so far—a significant departure in the history of by-elections in Tamil Nadu. All local leaders of the three main contesting parties—the TVK, the AIADMK, and the DMK—are also clear that it is unlikely that voters will be bribed this time around.

The Madras High Court, on September 16, termed the resignation of MLAs to join another party and subsequently recontest the same seats a “mockery of democracy”. Justice S.M. Subramaniam said: “An elected MLA resigning from his/her post, only to re-contest on behalf of another political party in the consequent by-election, may amount to insulting the voters and the choice they had made in the first instance.” The Division Bench (Subramaniam, along with K. Govindarajan) was of the view that the Election Commission of India should study this issue and use its powers granted under the Constitution’s Article 324 and draw up guidelines. Justice Subramaniam also made it clear that an MLA resigning his or her seat is an individual decision. But his concern was about the ethics of the same MLA contesting the same seat in the by-election caused by his/her resignation.
